content: Phimosis is a condition where the foreskin cannot be fully retracted past the head of the penis. It is often treated surgically through circumcision or prepuce plasty. However, non-invasive treatments using topical corticosteroids applied for four to eight weeks have shown promising results. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of topical corticosteroids applied to the narrowed portion of the foreskin in boys with phimosis, compared to placebo or no treatment. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared topical corticosteroids with placebo or no treatment in boys with any type or degree of phimosis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and ClinicalTrials.gov, with the last search performed on October 4, 2023. There were no language restrictions. In this updated review, two new studies with 111 participants were added, bringing the total to 14 studies involving 1459 randomized participants. The studies varied significantly in terms of the types of corticosteroids used, the age of participants, the degree and type of phimosis, and the duration of treatment. The findings suggest that topical corticosteroids may increase the likelihood of complete resolution of phimosis after four to eight weeks of treatment compared to placebo or no treatment. The risk ratio (RR) was 2.73 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.79 to 4.16), based on 10 trials with 834 participants. This corresponds to 436 more complete resolutions per 1000 boys treated with corticosteroids, compared to the control group. However, the certainty of this evidence was rated as low due to serious study limitations and inconsistency among the results. Topical corticosteroids may also increase the likelihood of partial resolution of phimosis after four to eight weeks of treatment. The RR was 1.68 (95% CI 1.17 to 2.40), based on 7 trials with 745 participants. This corresponds to 202 more partial resolutions per 1000 boys treated with corticosteroids, compared to the control group. Again, the certainty of the evidence was rated as low due to study limitations and inconsistency. The effect of topical corticosteroids on changes in retractability scores is uncertain. The standardized mean difference (SMD) was −1.48 (95% CI −2.93 to −0.03), based on 2 trials with 177 participants. The certainty of this evidence was rated as very low due to serious study limitations, heterogeneity, and imprecision. Topical corticosteroids may increase the likelihood of long-term complete resolution of phimosis six or more months after treatment. The RR was 4.09 (95% CI 2.80 to 5.97), based on 2 trials with 280 participants. This corresponds to 528 more complete resolutions per 1000 boys treated with corticosteroids, compared to the control group. The certainty of this evidence was rated as low due to study limitations and imprecision. There appears to be little or no difference in the risk of adverse effects between topical corticosteroids and placebo or no treatment. The RR was 0.28 (95% CI 0.03 to 2.62), based on 11 trials with 1091 participants. Only two of the 11 studies that recorded adverse effects reported any events, with one event occurring in the corticosteroid group and six in the control group. The certainty of this evidence was rated as low due to study limitations and imprecision. In conclusion, topical corticosteroids may increase both complete and partial resolution of phimosis after four to eight weeks of treatment and may also increase long-term complete resolution after six or more months. The risk of adverse effects appears to be minimal. However, the evidence is limited by poor reporting of study methods, clinical heterogeneity, and imprecision in the results. Higher-quality trials with long-term follow-up are needed to better understand the effects of topical corticosteroids on phimosis in boys.
